documents.title: Questions & Answers on the AI Act
documents.implementation_notes: This document is a Q&A/FAQ published by the European Commission explaining the EU AI Act (Regulation). The underlying AI Act is binding law; this document itself is regulatory guidance/explanatory material. Application dates are phased: prohibitions from 2 Feb 2025, GPAI rules from 2 Aug 2025, high-risk rules from 2 Aug 2026 (potentially delayed per Digital Omnibus proposal), Annex II products from 2 Aug 2027. The GPAI Code of Practice is voluntary but can serve as a compliance demonstration tool.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document repeatedly centers fundamental rights as the primary justification for regulation, banning specific AI practices because they 'contravene EU values because they violate fundamental rights,' requiring fundamental rights impact assessments, and structuring the risk classification around the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. Consumer/public safety is a strong secondary frame, as health and safety risks are co-stated throughout. Innovation enablement and economic competitiveness appear as secondary justifications to show the regulation is balanced. Existential/systemic risk language appears specifically around GPAI models (CBRN attacks, loss of human control) but is not the dominant framing.

documents.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence
documents.issuing_body: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
documents.implementation_notes: Regulation entered into force 20 days after publication (1 August 2024) with phased applicability. Complements existing EU law on data protection, product safety, consumer protection, and employment. Does not affect GDPR or Directive 2016/680 obligations. European AI Office established within Commission to oversee GPAI models. Member States must designate national competent authorities.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The EU AI Act consistently frames AI governance as necessary to protect fundamental rights, democracy, rule of law, and human dignity as enshrined in the EU Charter. While economic competitiveness and innovation enablement are prominent secondary themes, the primary justification for regulation is the protection of rights and freedoms. The document repeatedly references the Charter of Fundamental Rights, human-centric AI, and protection of natural persons as the core rationale.

documents.title: Standardisation of the AI Act
documents.implementation_notes: This page describes the EU AI Act standardisation process led by CEN/CENELEC JTC 21. Standards are voluntary but create a presumption of conformity. The first harmonised standard (prEN 18286) entered public enquiry on 30 October 2025. Application of high-risk AI rules is linked to availability of support tools, with a latest deadline of 2 December 2027 (Annex III) or 2 August 2028 (Annex I). International alignment with ISO/IEC SC 42 is a stated priority.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document primarily frames AI standardisation as enabling innovation and global competitiveness through harmonised standards that foster trust, reduce compliance costs, and position the EU as a global benchmark-setter. While safety and fundamental rights are mentioned as underlying concerns of the AI Act, the standardisation page's own reasoning emphasises how standards support innovation, market acceptance, and the EU's leadership role.

documents.title: AI Pact
documents.implementation_notes: The AI Pact is a voluntary initiative preparatory to the binding EU AI Act. Pillar I is a knowledge-sharing community open to all stakeholders. Pillar II involves voluntary pledges by providers and deployers. More than 230 companies have signed pledges. Reporting on progress is invited but not legally mandated.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document frames AI governance primarily around ensuring trustworthy, safe AI systems and compliance with the AI Act's safety and transparency requirements. It emphasizes risk categorization, human oversight, and safeguards. Fundamental rights and innovation enablement appear as secondary frames.

documents.title: The Commission publishes guidelines on AI system definition to facilitate the first AI Act's rules application
documents.implementation_notes: Guidelines are explicitly non-binding (paragraph 7: 'The Guidelines are not binding'). Authoritative interpretation rests solely with the CJEU. Guidelines were adopted in parallel with Commission guidelines on prohibited AI practices. They clarify the seven-element definition of 'AI system' under Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and note that systems based solely on rules defined by natural persons or limited to basic data processing fall outside the AI system definition.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document frames AI governance as necessary to ensure 'a high level of protection of health, safety, and fundamental rights in the Union, including democracy and the rule of law.' This rights-protective framing is the primary stated rationale, paired with a secondary emphasis on promoting innovation and uptake of AI.

documents.title: Opinion 28/2024 on certain data protection aspects related to the processing of personal data in the context of AI models
documents.implementation_notes: This is an EDPB opinion issued under Article 64(2) GDPR at the request of the Irish SA. It provides interpretive guidance to supervisory authorities on: (1) when AI models trained on personal data can be considered anonymous; (2) how legitimate interest as a legal basis applies to AI model development and deployment; (3) consequences of unlawful processing in development phase on subsequent processing. The opinion is addressed to SAs to inform their case-by-case assessments, but is without prejudice to controller obligations under GDPR. Not a binding regulation but carries significant weight as an EDPB opinion under the consistency mechanism.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document is a data protection opinion by the EDPB that frames AI governance squarely around the fundamental right to data protection (Article 8 EU Charter) and related rights such as privacy, freedom of expression, non-discrimination, and dignity. Throughout, it evaluates AI model processing through the lens of data subjects' rights and freedoms, the balancing of interests under GDPR, and the obligations of controllers to respect those rights. The justification for governance action is protecting individuals' fundamental rights from risks posed by AI model development and deployment, not economic competitiveness or national security.

documents.title: Guidance on Generative AI, strengthening data protection in a rapidly changing digital era
documents.implementation_notes: This is Version 2 of EDPS guidance issued under Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 (EUDPR), applicable specifically to EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies (EUIs). The document is explicitly not issued under the AI Act market surveillance authority role. Enforcement is primarily through GDPR-style accountability mechanisms and EDPS supervisory authority rather than direct penalties. The guidance is non-prescriptive on technical measures but establishes baseline data protection compliance expectations for all stages of the generative AI lifecycle. Several referenced documents (e.g., EDPS Guidance for Risk Management for AI systems) are noted as forthcoming.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document is explicitly grounded in data protection as a fundamental right. Its stated purpose is ensuring that EUIs comply with Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 to protect individuals' fundamental rights and freedoms when using generative AI. Risks are consistently framed as threats to individual rights—privacy, accuracy, non-discrimination, automated decision-making—rather than as threats to national security or economic competitiveness.

documents.title: Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI Models: Copyright Chapter
documents.issuing_body: European Commission / AI Office – Working Group 1 (GPAI Code of Practice)
documents.implementation_notes: This is the Copyright Chapter of the broader GPAI Code of Practice, intended to help Signatories demonstrate compliance with Article 53(1)(c) of the EU AI Act. Adherence is voluntary and does not constitute compliance with Union copyright law per se. Measures are proportionate to provider size, with SME/startup considerations. A dynamic list of copyright-infringing websites will be maintained on an EU website to assist compliance with Measure 1.2.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document is primarily framed around protecting fundamental rights—specifically intellectual property rights enshrined in EU law—as the basis for AI governance obligations. The overarching objective explicitly references 'a high level of protection of health, safety, and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law.' The substantive measures are devoted to ensuring AI providers respect copyright and related rights of rightsholders. A secondary innovation-enablement frame is present through references to supporting innovation and accommodating SMEs/startups. Consumer/public safety appears marginally through output safeguard requirements.

documents.title: Questions and answers on the code of practice for General-Purpose AI
documents.implementation_notes: This document is a Q&A on a voluntary Code of Practice that helps providers demonstrate compliance with the binding AI Act. The Code itself does not impose new obligations but serves as a compliance pathway. Full enforcement with fines begins August 2026; models pre-dating August 2025 have until August 2027. The systemic risk threshold is set at 10^25 FLOPs of training compute.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document primarily frames AI governance around ensuring that general-purpose AI models placed on the EU market are safe and transparent, with special attention to systemic risk from the most powerful models. The core justification is protecting users and society from unsafe models, framed through compliance with the AI Act's safety and transparency obligations. Secondary frames include fundamental rights (copyright protections) and innovation enablement (streamlined compliance, reduced administrative burden, good-faith enforcement transition).

documents.title: Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI Models: Safety and Security Chapter
documents.implementation_notes: This Code of Practice is a voluntary instrument under the EU AI Act. Adherence serves as a means for providers to demonstrate compliance with Articles 53 and 55 AI Act obligations, but does not constitute conclusive evidence of compliance. SMEs and SMCs may benefit from simplified compliance paths including exemptions from some reporting commitments per Article 56(5) AI Act. The document is the Safety and Security Chapter specifically, focused on systemic risk assessment and mitigation across the model lifecycle.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document primarily frames AI governance around protecting public health, safety, and fundamental rights from systemic risks posed by general-purpose AI models. The overarching objective explicitly references 'high level of protection of health, safety, and fundamental rights' and systemic risks defined as those with 'significant impact...on public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, or the society as a whole.' Safety and security mitigations, systemic risk assessments, and mandatory reporting all center on preventing harms to users and society. Fundamental rights and social stability appear as strong secondary frames, with innovation enablement also present through the 'Principle of Innovation in AI Safety and Security.'

documents.title: Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI Models: Transparency Chapter
documents.issuing_body: European Commission / AI Office (Working Group 1, Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI Models)
documents.implementation_notes: This is a voluntary Code of Practice under Article 53 AI Act. Adherence does not constitute conclusive evidence of compliance with AI Act obligations. Open-source model providers are exempt from Measures 1.1-1.3 unless the model poses systemic risk. Confidentiality protections apply per Article 78 AI Act. A fillable Model Documentation Form is provided as a compliance tool.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document frames AI governance primarily around protecting fundamental rights, health, safety, democracy, and the rule of law as enshrined in the EU Charter, in alignment with the AI Act's stated objectives. Transparency obligations are justified by the need to enable regulatory oversight, protect rights of downstream users, and ensure trustworthy AI. Secondary framings include consumer/public safety (high-risk AI system compliance) and innovation enablement (supporting AI uptake and market functioning).

documents.title: Guidelines for providers of general-purpose AI models
documents.implementation_notes: Guidelines are explicitly stated as 'not legally binding' but reflect the Commission's interpretation and will guide enforcement. Enforcement powers (including fines) enter into application 2 August 2026. Providers of models placed on market before 2 August 2025 have until 2 August 2027 to comply. The GPAI Code of Practice is a complementary voluntary tool.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document primarily frames AI governance as enabling confident innovation through clarity and pragmatic obligations. Repeated emphasis on helping actors 'innovate with confidence,' exemptions for open-source to 'promote transparency and innovation,' and the stated EU approach of promoting 'excellence and trust' while boosting 'research and industrial capacity' signals an innovation-enablement framing. Safety and fundamental rights appear as secondary justifications.

documents.title: Guidelines on the scope of the obligations for providers of GPAI models
documents.implementation_notes: Guidelines issued under Article 96(1) of the AI Act. They clarify key concepts (what constitutes a GPAI model, provider, placing on the market, computational resources for training) and how the AI Office will support providers. Part of a broader package including the GPAI Code of Practice, adequacy assessment, transparency template for training data, and notification template for systemic-risk providers. Guidelines approved in content on 18 July 2025 but formal adoption deferred pending all language versions; only binding/applicable from formal adoption date.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document explicitly states the AI Act's aim is to promote innovation while 'ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights, including democracy and the rule of law.' The rights-based framing is primary, though innovation enablement is strongly co-present.

documents.title: Vademecum of the GPAI Signatory Taskforce
documents.issuing_body: European AI Office / Signatory Taskforce of the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
documents.implementation_notes: This Vademecum governs the internal organisation and operation of the Signatory Taskforce under the GPAI Code of Practice, which was assessed as adequate pursuant to Article 56(6) of the AI Act. It is not itself a binding instrument but structures voluntary cooperation among signatories. The AI Office chairs the Taskforce and may publish the Vademecum, participant lists, and high-level meeting minutes under its transparency obligations. Decisions are taken by consensus with a default agreement period of no less than 10 working days.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document is primarily procedural, establishing the governance structure of a Signatory Taskforce for the GPAI Code of Practice under the EU AI Act. The dominant framing is innovation enablement — the taskforce exists to facilitate cooperative implementation of the Code, exchange views on technological developments, and adapt guidance to market and technological changes. Safety and rights concerns appear implicitly through references to the 'risk landscape' and 'societal developments,' but are secondary to enabling structured industry participation and code compliance.

documents.title: Commission publishes the Guidelines on prohibited artificial intelligence (AI) practices, as defined by the AI Act.
documents.implementation_notes: These are Commission guidelines interpreting Article 5 of the EU AI Act on prohibited practices. They are not themselves binding law but provide the Commission's interpretation. Ireland and Denmark have opt-out provisions for certain RBI prohibitions. Prohibitions apply to placing on market, putting into service, and use, including misuse. General-purpose AI systems are covered. Continuous compliance throughout AI lifecycle is required.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document consistently frames AI governance around protecting fundamental rights, democracy, rule of law, and human dignity. The risk classification system centers on 'unacceptable risks to fundamental rights and Union values.' Harms are analyzed in terms of physical, psychological, and societal impacts on individuals' rights and freedoms. Innovation enablement is a secondary but explicit goal.

documents.title: Request for an article 64(2) opinion from the IE SA on AI models
documents.implementation_notes: This is a request by the Irish SA to the EDPB for an Article 64(2) GDPR opinion on AI model data processing questions. It is not itself a binding decision or guidance document; it poses questions for EDPB harmonisation. Explicitly limited to GDPR/LED application only, excluding the AI Act, DMA, DGA, DSA interplay.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document is centrally framed around data subjects' fundamental rights under GDPR. The IE SA's request focuses on ensuring lawful processing of personal data in AI model development, protecting data subjects across the EU/EEA from rights violations, and achieving harmonized enforcement of data protection law. The language consistently foregrounds data subject rights, legal bases for processing, and compliance obligations rather than economic competitiveness, security threats, or societal disruption.

documents.title: Template for the public summary of training content of GPAI models
documents.implementation_notes: This document is a template and explanatory notice issued by the AI Office under Article 53(1)(d) of the EU AI Act, requiring all GPAI model providers to publish a public summary of training content. The template has three sections: general information, list of data sources, and relevant data processing aspects. Providers may voluntarily disclose more than the minimum required. The open-source exception under Article 53(2) does not apply to this obligation. A voluntary 'upon request' mechanism for rightsholders regarding domain names not listed in the summary is recommended but not mandatory.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document frames training data transparency primarily as a mechanism to protect and enable the exercise of fundamental rights under EU law, including intellectual property rights, data subject rights, non-discrimination, cultural diversity, freedom of information, and freedom of science. Governance obligations are justified by enabling rightsholders and affected parties to exercise and enforce their legal rights.

documents.title: Template for general-purpose AI model providers to summarise their training content
documents.implementation_notes: Template use is mandatory under Article 53(1)(d) of the AI Act. Obligation applies from 2 August 2025 for new models; existing models have until 2 August 2027. Enforcement actions possible from 2 August 2026. Applies to open-source model providers as well. Code of Practice adherence remains voluntary and addresses separate obligations.
documents.framing_rationale_summary: The document frames AI governance primarily around enabling rights-holders to exercise their legal rights—copyright, data protection, non-discrimination, consumer protection—under Union law. The core justification for the transparency obligation is that parties with legitimate interests need information to assert their rights, not safety or competitiveness concerns.
